title: The Fashionable Suite
program_note:
The Fashionable Suite was written between October, 1986 and November, 1987. The first, The Fashionable Drag, was written from October to November, 1986. The second, Piano Bells, was begun in November, 1986, and completed, along with the last, Ellipses, in November, 1987.

All three pieces are basically minimalist in flavor, and are each concerned, in a different way, with the chromatic whole. Thus, in exhibiting two of the twentieth century’s musical “fashions,” the Suite has become a “fashionable” one. The Fashionable Drag also features stride-like writing, characteristic of ragtime music—another one of the many musical fashions of the past 100 years. All movements employ various minimalist techniques, including phasing, repetition, progressive augmentation, and slow changes, overall.

The Fashionable Drag is not really a “real slow drag”—being in triple, rather than duple meter, it is more of a fast waltz—but it does evoke the style of such drags. Phasing is the most important technique employed in this piece, along with a layering technique that ultimately gives rise to five different lines in the contrapuntal texture in the last eight bars.

Piano Bells is neither played on bells, nor is it predominantly soft or piano. But the concentration on the interval of a fifth and the percussive nature of this piece should combine to produce a bell-like sound. A long middle section leaves the bell-like fifths for harmonic collections of fifths: two different pentatonic collections. This interest in pentatonic collections is picked up in Ellipses.

Ellipses is characterized by circular or elliptical movements away from and back towards a starting point. It is the simplest of the three movements—rarely having more than two lines at one time, and is concerned with the chromatic whole mostly through the pentatonic collections that are presented in just about every bar.

Total duration is approximately twelve minutes: the individual movements are approximately three, four, and five minutes, respectively. The Fashionable Drag uses a wide range of the piano; Piano Bells and Ellipses use a much narrower range. Both the sostenuto pedal and the damper pedal are called for in the first movement. The damper pedal is called for in the other two. The performer should feel free to add pedaling to his or her own taste where it is not otherwise indicated.

David S. Lefkowitz

3 December, 1987

Philadelphia, PA
